en: Udāna 3.3 Yasojasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, about five hundred monks headed by Yasoja had arrived at Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One.
As those visiting monks were exchanging greetings with the resident monks, and were preparing their lodgings and putting away their bowls and robes, they made a loud noise and a great clamor.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, what is this loud noise, this great clamor? It sounds like fishermen over a haul of fish.
“Venerable sir, these are about five hundred bhikkhus, headed by Yasoja, who have arrived at Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One.”
“Those visiting bhikkhus, while exchanging greetings with the resident bhikkhus and putting away their lodgings and robes, are making a loud noise, a great clamor.
“In that case, Ānanda, address those bhikkhus in my name, saying:
‘The Teacher calls upon you, venerable sirs.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. He then approached those bhikkhus and said to them, “The Teacher summons you, friends.
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda, and they approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As those bhikkhus were sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to them:
"Why is it, bhikkhus, that you are making such a loud noise, such a great clamor, like fishermen over a haul of fish?"
When this was said, the Venerable Yasoja said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, these five hundred bhikkhus have arrived at Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One.
These visiting bhikkhus, while exchanging greetings with the resident bhikkhus, and while preparing lodgings and putting away their bowls and robes, are making a loud noise, a great clamor.”
“Go, bhikkhus, I dismiss you; you are not to dwell in my presence.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.

Then, rising from their seats, they paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to their right, set their lodgings in order, took their bowls and robes, and set out on tour toward the Vajjis.
Wandering on tour among the Vajjis in due course, they approached the river Vaggumudā. Having approached it, they made leaf-huts on the bank of the river Vaggumudā and entered the rains retreat.
Then, having entered the rains retreat, the Venerable Yasoja addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, we have been sent away by the Blessed One, who desires our welfare, seeks our benefit, and out of compassion has taken pity on us."
"Come, friends, let us dwell in such a way that the Blessed One will be pleased with us as we dwell.
"Very well, friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Yasoja.
Then, dwelling secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, all those monks realized the three knowledges within that very same rainy season.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Sāvatthī for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Vesālī.
Traveling by stages on his journey, he arrived at Vesālī.
There, the Blessed One stayed in the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest at Vesālī.
Then the Blessed One, having encompassed with his own mind the minds of the monks dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā River and having reflected upon them, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, this direction has become as if filled with light to me; Ānanda, this direction has become as if filled with radiance to me;
in the direction where the monks dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā reside, it is not disagreeable for me to direct my attention.”
“Ānanda, you should send a messenger to the bhikkhus dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā River, saying:
‘The Teacher calls upon the venerable ones; the Teacher desires to see the venerable ones.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Having done so, he approached a certain bhikkhu and said to him:
“Come, friend, go to where the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā River are; having approached them, say to the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā:
‘The Teacher calls upon you, venerable sirs; the Teacher desires to see you.
“Very well, friend,” that monk replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so,
vanishing from the peaked-roofed hall in the Great Forest, he reappeared before those bhikkhus on the bank of the Vaggumudā River.
Then that bhikkhu said this to the bhikkhus dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā:
“The Teacher calls for you; the Teacher desires to see you, venerable sirs.

“Very well, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to that bhikkhu. Having put their lodgings in order and taking their bowls and robes, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, they vanished from that place.
In this very way, having vanished from the bank of the Vaggumudā River, they reappeared in the presence of the Blessed One in the Gabled Hall within the Great Forest.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was seated in the imperturbable concentration (*āneñja-samādhi*).
Then, it occurred to those bhikkhus:
“By what dwelling does the Blessed One dwell at present?
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
“The Blessed One now dwells by means of the imperturbable dwelling.”
They all sat down with imperturbable concentration.

Then, when the night was far advanced and the first watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
"The night, Bhante, has far advanced; the first watch has passed; these visiting bhikkhus have been sitting for a long time."
“May the Blessed One, venerable sir, exchange greetings with the visiting bhikkhus.
When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.

A second time, when the night had advanced and the middle watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Venerable sir, the night has passed;
the middle watch has ended;
these visiting bhikkhus have been sitting for a long time.”
"May the Blessed One, venerable sir, exchange greetings with the visiting bhikkhus.
A second time, the Blessed One remained silent.
And a third time, when the night was far spent and the last watch had passed, the Venerable Ānanda rose.
When the night had turned to dawn, Aruṇa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder,
and extending his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
“The night has passed, Bhante.”
The final watch has passed;
the dawn has broken;
the night has a joyful face.
“Bhante, the visiting monks have been sitting for a long time;
let the Blessed One exchange greetings with the visiting monks.
Then the Blessed One, having emerged from that concentration, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“If you had known this, Ānanda, you would not have said even so much.
Both I, Ānanda, and these five hundred bhikkhus were all seated in imperturbable concentration.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the significance of this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“He for whom the thorn of sensual desire,
as well as abuse, killing, and bondage have been conquered—
like a mountain, he stands unshaken.”
He does not tremble in the face of pleasure and pain—he is a bhikkhu. Thus ends the third [sutta].
